entries.clue: Brilliant goddess in wood (4-4)

indicatorNotes.in: In puts the word before it inside the word after it, rather than alongside.

blocks.note: fir is a timber, and it opens after two letters to take the insertion
Vesta is the Roman goddess of the hearth, tended by the vestal virgins

annotation.surface: A dazzling goddess standing among the trees.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wood' wants to be the forest the goddess is standing in; it is the timber, and only a three-letter one is short enough to wrap round her. Ratings of hotels and films run up to five stars.
annotation.definitionFit: Five-star is the top grade a hotel or a performance can be given, so it carries the sense of outstanding that brilliant does.

entries.clue: Anthem: keen on it when rector enters (7)

indicatorNotes.enters: Whoever enters goes inside, so that letter is placed within the words already written out.

blocks.note: to be keen on something is, colloquially, to be into it
the word itself, written out after the first piece
R is the abbreviation for rector on a parish noticeboard

annotation.surface: A hymn struck up the moment the rector walks in.
annotation.walkthrough: An introit is the psalm sung while the priest approaches the altar, so the rector arriving is exactly when it starts. 'Keen on' has to be heard as the colloquial 'into' before anything comes apart.
annotation.definitionFit: The introit is the sung piece that opens a church service, the choir's first anthem of the morning.

entries.clue: Woman cold in rising river (5)

indicatorNotes.in: In sets the letter before it inside the water that follows rather than beside it.
indicatorNotes.rising: Something rising is travelling upwards, and in a down entry that means reading the letters from the bottom of the column up.

blocks.note: the Aire is a Yorkshire river, running through Leeds, and it climbs the column here
C is cold, the letter on the tap

annotation.surface: A woman shivering as the river rises around her.
annotation.walkthrough: A rising river is a flood in the surface and an instruction in the parse. Erica is the woman's name and also the botanical name for heather, which is why it looks less like a name than it is.
annotation.definitionFit: Erica is an ordinary woman's given name in Britain, the Latin word for heather pressed into service as one.

entries.clue: Dramatic effect in Goethe a treat (7)

indicatorNotes.in: In says the answer is sitting inside the letters that follow, not described by what they mean.

blocks.note: the run crosses two gaps: the end of GoeTHE, then A, then the start of TREat

annotation.surface: Goethe's plays being recommended as a treat.
annotation.walkthrough: Goethe wrote for the stage, so his name next to 'a treat' reads as praise rather than as a run of letters. Hidden words that straddle two word breaks are the hardest to see.
annotation.definitionFit: A sense of theatre is the staged, showy quality of a gesture, which is what dramatic effect names.

entries.clue: Succeed in getting runs singly (5)

blocks.note: r is runs on a cricket scorecard
things taken singly are taken each in turn

annotation.surface: A batsman getting his runs one at a time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Singly' looks like a hint to take one letter and is doing the work of a whole word. The R beside it is the cricket scorer's, which is what lets the surface stay on the pitch.
annotation.definitionFit: To reach a total or a place is to succeed in getting to it, the verb taking the same object either way.

entries.clue: Slightly opening case from Hastings customs (6)

indicatorNotes.opening: Opening something parts it, and the parted halves leave a gap for what goes inside.
indicatorNotes.case from: A case is what encloses a thing, so the case from a word is its outermost letters.

blocks.note: the outside letters of HastingS, the case the rest is packed into
slightly is a bit, run together as four letters

annotation.surface: An officer at Hastings easing open a case just a crack.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Customs' ends the clue looking like the men in the shed at the port, and is the definition, meaning settled practices. Hastings is a fishing town on the Sussex coast, the one the 1066 battle is named after.
annotation.definitionFit: Habits are the things a person does from long practice without deciding to, which is what customs in the plural names.

entries.clue: Spanish nobleman concealed a large repair (7)

blocks.note: concealed in the past tense is hid
the word itself, taken straight from the clue
L is the large size on a clothing label
in the older sense, to repair to the drawing room is to go there

annotation.surface: A Spanish gentleman quietly hiding the fact that a big repair is needed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Repair' is the trap: nothing is being mended, and the verb is the old one for taking yourself somewhere. A hidalgo is a gentleman of the lesser Spanish nobility, the rank Don Quixote holds.
annotation.definitionFit: Hidalgo is the Spanish title for a man of the lower nobility, entitled to the don but not to a great estate.

entries.clue: Internal regulator's lad checking D-Notice? (4,5)

indicatorNotes.checking: To check a thing is to hold it back, and the word doing the holding closes round what it stops.

blocks.note: a lad is a boy, and he opens after two letters
the letter exactly as the clue prints it
to clock something is British slang for noticing it

annotation.surface: A young man vetting a government order not to publish.
annotation.walkthrough: A D-Notice is the request British governments send editors asking them not to print something on security grounds, which is why the letter and the word are hyphenated together. Only one of the two belongs to the parse.
annotation.definitionFit: The body clock is the internal rhythm that decides when you sleep, wake and feel hungry, regulating the body with no instruction from you.

entries.clue: See 13
A bigot rolled with rugger match in disorder (2,5,3,6)

indicatorNotes.rolled: Something rolled has been turned right over, so the word beside it is written back to front.

blocks.note: the word itself, standing at the front
a bigot is a sexist, the six letters turned over
with joins two things together, and so does AND
sevens is the seven-a-side form of rugby union, played as its own tournament

annotation.surface: A bigot knocked flat at a rugby match that has descended into chaos.
annotation.walkthrough: Nothing in the surface counts anything: the first number comes out of a word for bigot written backwards. 'With' looks like a joiner and is really three letters spelt out.
annotation.definitionFit: To be at sixes and sevens is to be muddled and all over the place, the state in disorder describes.

entries.clue: Italian poet losing heart in court (4)

indicatorNotes.losing: To lose something is to be left without it, so the letter named alongside drops out of the word.

blocks.note: Dante Alighieri, who wrote the Divine Comedy
a five-letter word has one middle letter, and that is its heart

annotation.surface: An Italian poet downhearted at his appearance in court.
annotation.walkthrough: Dante is the poet crossword clues mean by 'Italian poet', and the surface's courtroom hides the other sense of court, the old-fashioned business of taking somebody out.
annotation.definitionFit: To date someone is to court them: both verbs mean going about together with romance in view.

entries.clue: Screen hero in Slough works (6)

blocks.note: a slough is a patch of soft waterlogged ground, a bog
the works hanging in a gallery are art

annotation.surface: A film star being shown round a factory in Slough.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital letter makes Slough the Berkshire town; the setter wants the common noun underneath it. Humphrey Bogart played Rick in Casablanca and Sam Spade in The Maltese Falcon.
annotation.definitionFit: Humphrey Bogart was the hard-boiled leading man of Casablanca and The Big Sleep, about as much a hero of the screen as anyone.

entries.clue: Cynical outlook reported in most recent epoch? (8)

indicatorNotes.reported: What is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so it is the sound of the phrase that matters and not its spelling.

blocks.note: cynical gives hollow, empty of any real feeling, and an outlook is a scene; spoken together they are two words, written down they are one

annotation.surface: Somebody's jaundiced view of the world being reported in our own geological age.
annotation.walkthrough: The Holocene is the epoch that began when the last ice age ended, about 11,700 years ago, and we are still in it. The sound wanted is a two-word phrase, which is why counting syllables gets you nowhere.
annotation.definitionFit: The Holocene is the current geological epoch, the most recent division of the timescale, running from the end of the last ice age to now.

entries.clue: Why blame for Strictly row should be shared? (2,5,3,2,5)

annotation.definition: Why blame for Strictly row should be shared?

blocks.note: the surface asks who started the bust-up on Strictly Come Dancing, the BBC's Saturday-night ballroom contest, which is why the title is in italics
the proverb's own answer: a quarrel, like the dance the show exists to put on, cannot be managed alone, so neither party is innocent

annotation.surface: Wondering aloud why the blame for a Strictly bust-up should fall on both parties.
annotation.walkthrough: The tango is danced on Strictly every autumn, so the programme supplies the dance and the row supplies the two. The answer runs on into 8 down.
annotation.definitionFit: The proverb says nobody quarrels alone, and it says so by naming a dance that needs a partner, which is what the show is for.

entries.clue: Poor emaciated in compound (9)

indicatorNotes.Poor: A poor specimen of anything is a botched one, with its parts not in the state they should be.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A half-starved prisoner in a guarded compound.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Compound' is the walled enclosure the surface needs and the chemical one the answer is. Poor and emaciated sit together so naturally that neither of them looks like an instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Acetamide is a chemical compound, the amide made from acetic acid, used as a solvent and a plasticiser.

entries.clue: Away from West for digital process? (3)

blocks.note: heading away from one compass point is heading TO another
the point opposite West is East, e on the compass rose

annotation.surface: Moving away from the West as part of some computerised procedure.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Digital' points at computers in the surface and at fingers and toes in the answer. A process, in anatomy, is any projecting part of the body, which is what the question mark is covering.
annotation.definitionFit: Toes are the digits of the foot, and process is anatomy's word for a part that sticks out from the rest.

entries.clue: Order parts for ordinary instrument (4)

indicatorNotes.parts: When something parts it opens up in the middle, leaving room between the halves.

blocks.note: the OBE is the Order of the British Empire, handed out in the honours list
O stands for ordinary in British exam grades

annotation.surface: Putting in an order for parts for an unremarkable instrument.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Order parts' reads as a stores requisition, which is the one thing it is not. The O comes from the old O-level, the exam English teenagers sat at sixteen before GCSEs arrived.
annotation.definitionFit: The oboe is the double-reed woodwind that gives the orchestra its tuning A before a concert.

entries.clue: See 27
Near enough furious about nationalist's introduction (2,5)

indicatorNotes.about: Putting one thing about another wraps it round, so the letter named goes inside.

blocks.note: somebody furious is in rage
the introduction to a word is its opening letter, here the N of nationalist

annotation.surface: A nationalist's opening remarks leaving somebody close to fury.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Near enough' reads as the British shrug meaning roughly right, and means within reach, the way a target is. The N is the first letter of the word in the clue rather than the usual abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: Something in range is close enough to be reached or hit, which is the near enough the definition means.

entries.clue: Unique sort against an enemy turned King in with Duke (3,2,1,4)

indicatorNotes.turned: Someone turned has been faced the other way round, so those letters are written back to front.

blocks.note: leaning on a wall is leaning against it
an enemy is A FOE, the article included and the pair written backwards
K is the king in chess notation and on a playing card
the word itself, spelt out
d is the abbreviation for duke in peerage listings

annotation.surface: An unusual character ranged against an enemy who has gone over to the King.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like an order to put one thing inside another and is two letters written out, which is what keeps the charade from falling open. The reversal takes the article with it.
annotation.definitionFit: A one-of-a-kind is a thing no second example of exists, which is what calling something a unique sort claims.

entries.clue: Repose in old French art for Greek matricide (7)

indicatorNotes.in: In drops the word before it inside the letters that follow.

blocks.note: o is the standard abbreviation for old
repose is rest, the noun for the state of lying quiet
art is the archaic English 'you are', and the French for that is es

annotation.surface: A moment of repose inside an old piece of French art.
annotation.walkthrough: 'French art' is a gallery in the surface and a verb in the parse: art is the thou form of to be, and es is its French twin. Orestes killed his mother Clytemnestra to avenge his father Agamemnon.
annotation.definitionFit: Orestes is the Greek who murdered his own mother, a killing the tragedians went back to again and again.

entries.clue: German woman holding seance regularly for US poet ()

indicatorNotes.holding: What holds something keeps it within itself, so the letters picked out go inside the other word.
indicatorNotes.regularly: Letters taken regularly come at a steady interval, which in practice means every second one.

blocks.note: Frau is the German for woman, and the German for Mrs
the second, fourth and sixth letters of sEaNcE

annotation.surface: A German woman running regular seances.
annotation.walkthrough: Philip Freneau, called the poet of the American Revolution, wrote satirical verse against the British in the 1770s. Even letters rather than odd ones are what 'regularly' asks for here.
annotation.definitionFit: Philip Freneau was an American poet of the Revolutionary period, writing in the cause of the new republic.

entries.clue: No explosive energy in runner (7)

blocks.note: the word itself, opening the charade
a mine is the explosive buried in a field or moored at sea
E is energy in physics, the letter in Einstein's equation

annotation.surface: A sprinter with no explosive energy left in the closing stages.
annotation.walkthrough: Explosive energy is exactly what a sprinter is said to have, so the phrase reads as one idea instead of three pieces. The runner here is running for office.
annotation.definitionFit: A nominee is somebody put forward for a post or a prize, and a candidate of that kind is said to be running for it.

entries.clue: Way through Scots mountains becomes wider (8)

indicatorNotes.through: A way that goes through something passes inside it, so those letters land in the middle.

blocks.note: a ben is a Scottish mountain, the word in Ben Nevis and Ben Lomond
a way is a road, as street names still use it

annotation.surface: A route through the Scottish hills opening out.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word of this one can be read straight, which is what makes it hard: the definition is the last two words, a verb and not a comparison. Ben is the Gaelic beinn, worn down.
annotation.definitionFit: A road that broadens becomes wider, the verb meaning to grow in breadth rather than to make something broad.

entries.clue: Something added to letters in sacks sent north (5)

indicatorNotes.sent north: North is up the page, so in a down entry the letters are written from the bottom upwards.

blocks.note: to sack an employee is to fire them, and FIRES climbs the column

annotation.surface: Extra items slipped into mailbags heading north.
annotation.walkthrough: The letters are type rather than post, and the sacks are dismissals rather than bags, so both halves of the picture have to be given up at once. Sans-serif faces are the ones without these strokes.
annotation.definitionFit: A serif is the small finishing stroke on the stems of a printed letter, the detail a sans-serif typeface leaves off.

entries.clue: Quarters affected? Pitch tents (6)

blocks.note: east and north are two of the compass's four quarters
camp is the word for a manner that is exaggerated and put on

annotation.surface: With the barracks out of action, the soldiers are told to pitch tents.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Quarters' is soldiers' lodgings in the surface and points of the compass in the parse, two of them. The joke is that the affected word sits inside the answer unchanged.
annotation.definitionFit: To encamp is to settle down in tents for a night or a season, which is what pitching tents amounts to.

entries.clue: Drop a little lower keeping length in mind (5)

indicatorNotes.keeping: To keep a thing is to hold on to it, so the word doing the keeping closes round what it holds.

blocks.note: cave! is British schoolboy Latin for look out, so it means mind or beware
l is length in a measurement, as in l x w x h

annotation.surface: A coach telling someone to drop a little lower and keep the length in mind.
annotation.walkthrough: A lower is a cow, the beast that lows, so a little lower is a calf; dropping one is the stockman's verb for giving birth to it. Cave was shouted in British schools when a master approached.
annotation.definitionFit: To calve is to give birth to a calf, and farmers call that dropping one, a calf being a small animal that lows.

entries.clue: Opponent pawns this occasionally (4)

indicatorNotes.occasionally: Something done occasionally happens every so often instead of all the time, so only every other letter is taken.

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of pAwNs ThIs

annotation.surface: A chess opponent who pushes a pawn now and then.
annotation.walkthrough: 'This' looks like a pointer at the answer and is four letters of the fodder, two of them the ones wanted. An anti is a noun here: one of the antis, somebody set against whatever is proposed.
annotation.definitionFit: An anti is a person ranged against a proposal, the noun made straight out of the preposition, which is what an opponent is.

entries.clue: Credit Blenheim for rearranging detailed figures? (5,5,4)

indicatorNotes.rearranging: Rearranging something keeps every part of it and puts those parts in a different order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, fourteen letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Giving Blenheim the credit for sorting out a set of itemised accounts.
annotation.walkthrough: Blenheim Palace was the nation's thank-you to the Duke of Marlborough, and 'detailed figures' is the sort of phrase that turns up in the accounts next to it. The answer runs on into 17 across.
annotation.definitionFit: In the nursery rhyme the farmer's wife cuts off the mice's tails, leaving them de-tailed, and three is itself a figure.

entries.clue: See 9
Fish indeed chasing drunken Scots about (4-4)

indicatorNotes.chasing: To chase is to come along behind, so those letters are written after the ones they follow.

blocks.note: fou is the Scots word for drunk, the one Burns uses
re means about, the heading at the top of a memo
indeed agrees with what has just been said, and so does yes

annotation.surface: Fish, right enough, following a party of drunken Scots around.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is a real creature, the anableps, whose divided eyes watch above and below the waterline at the same time. 'Drunken' looks like an instruction to jumble and is part of a straight definition.
annotation.definitionFit: The four-eyes is a tropical freshwater fish named for the split eyes that let it see into the air and the water at once.
